title: The thief who kept the lamp lit
hookLine: a thief turns up Shiva's lamp on Shivaratri night, and the Rudram's namah bows even to the lord of thieves
carry: namah: the bow leaves no one out
tomorrow: eldest or youngest: whose bow is louder?

cards: Gunanidhi was a learned man's son who became a gambler and a thief, and was thrown out of his home.
On Shivaratri night, the Shiva Purana says, he crept, starving, into a Shiva temple, where devotees had left food and fallen asleep. The lamp was going out.
So he could see to steal, he tore a strip from his cloth, made a new wick and turned the flame up bright. He grabbed the food, someone woke, he ran, and that night he was killed.

teach.b: Then the story turns. Death's messengers come for him, and Shiva's own attendants stop them. Without meaning to, Gunanidhi had fasted, kept awake and kept Shiva's lamp burning on Shivaratri.

teach.h: NAMAH: A BOW, AGAIN AND AGAIN.
teach.b: He's born again as a king who lights lamps in Shiva's temples, and in time, the Purana says, becomes Kubera, the lord of wealth, Shiva's friend. Now listen to the sound the Rudram keeps making.
Namo, namah, like a drumbeat. Namah means a bow; it's the word inside namaste. Line after line of the Namakam is built the same way: namah, a name of Rudra, often cha, and.
And look who gets the bow. Carpenters and potters. Hunters, and dogs, and the keepers of dogs.
And yes, the line says it: a bow to the lord of thieves. The Rudram isn't praising stealing. It's saying there's no corner where Shiva isn't, so there's no one the bow skips.
That's a core Hindu teaching, and you can see it in the most ordinary gesture: palms together, a small bow, namaste. Many Hindus explain it as bowing to the divine in the other person.
A thief in a dark temple was still close enough to Shiva to turn up his light. So when someone cuts the line, snaps at you, takes what isn't theirs, the hymn doesn't say it's fine.
It says they're not outside the bow. Namah. I see you there, and I bow.

how: The Rudram is chanted in Vedic Sanskrit, with the namah lines carrying its rhythm; many Hindus keep Shivaratri with fasting, lamps and a night awake, and greet one another with palms together, namaste.

o: a Vedic hymn whose namah bows to everyone, even the lord of thieves
a Vedic hymn that names Rudra only once, at the start
a Vedic hymn that bows only to priests and kings

games.q: the bow that leaves no one out — tap the pairs.
p: the thief who kept the lamp lit

s: the Rudram bows even to the lord of thieves
stenanam pataye namah: no corner is outside Shiva.
the Rudram's bow to thieves praises stealing
it says no one is outside the bow, not that theft is fine.
Gunanidhi went into the temple to pray
he went to steal; he turned up the lamp only so he could see.

games.q: someone cuts the line at the temple. by the Rudram's teaching, are they outside the namah?
o: no: the bow leaves no one out.
games.why: the Rudram bows even to the lord of thieves. namah isn't approval; it's seeing Shiva there too.

practice: Put your palms together at your chest, the gesture of namaste. Bring to mind people from your week, one at a time: someone you love, someone you barely noticed, someone who annoyed you.
For each, bow your head a little and say namah, silently. If you pray, end with Om namah shivaya. If you don't, end with the meaning: I see you there, and I bow.

wordCard.voice: The Rudram. Today's word inside it: namah, a bow, said again and again until no one is left out, not even the lord of thieves.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a bow, homage. the word that carries the rhythm of the Rudram's Namakam.

carryVoice: Your line: namah, the bow leaves no one out. One small word, said again and again. A week walked.
